title: Build a decision tree, not a topic list
summary: A useful structure breaks the decision into distinct drivers and makes the first investigation obvious.
principles: Start with the decision and split it into a few independent drivers.
Make branches specific enough to test with evidence.
Name the branch you would investigate first and explain why.
example: For falling profit, separate revenue from cost before splitting price, volume, fixed cost, and variable cost.

title: Ask the question that can change the answer
summary: Prioritization is choosing the next question with the highest decision value, not collecting every available fact.
principles: Begin with the largest plausible driver of the outcome.
Prefer questions that distinguish between competing explanations.
Stop exploring a branch when the evidence makes it immaterial.
example: If margins fell sharply while sales stayed stable, test major cost categories before researching customer awareness.

title: Carry the math into the decision
summary: Correct arithmetic matters only when you translate the result into its business implication.
principles: State the formula and units before calculating.
Sense-check the scale and direction of the result.
Compare the answer with the decision threshold and say what changes.
example: A 12% margin is not just a result: against a 15% hurdle, it means the proposal is not yet viable.

title: Read exhibits in three moves
summary: Use What / So what / Now what to turn a chart observation into a focused next action.
principles: What: identify the strongest comparison or change without explaining it yet.
So what: connect that pattern to the case objective.
Now what: name the next question or analysis that would confirm the implication.
example: What: churn doubled in small accounts. So what: they drive the retention gap. Now what: test whether service delays explain their exits.

title: Synthesize around the decision
summary: A synthesis selects the few facts that alter the answer and uses them to direct the next move.
principles: Lead with the current answer, not a recap of the process.
Support it with two or three decisive facts.
Close with the unresolved risk or highest-value next step.
example: Profit pressure is cost-led, mainly overtime; validate the staffing and turnover link before recommending a labor intervention.

title: Segment where behavior differs
summary: A total can hide opposing stories. Split the problem only along dimensions that may change the decision.
principles: Choose segments with a reason to behave differently: customer, product, channel, region, or time.
Compare both size and performance so a dramatic but tiny segment does not distract you.
Avoid cuts that merely reorganize the same information.
example: Flat total growth can conceal enterprise gains offset by small-business losses, requiring different actions for each segment.

title: Separate performance from mix shift
summary: An average can move even when every segment is unchanged because the weight of high- and low-value segments changed.
principles: Inspect segment shares alongside segment-level performance.
Ask whether the overall change comes from within segments or between them.
Target the cause: fix segment economics or influence the mix.
example: Average price may fall with unchanged product prices when customers buy more entry-level products.

title: Find the hidden denominator
summary: Rates and averages can mislead when the population beneath them changes.
principles: Rewrite every rate as numerator divided by denominator.
Check whether either component changed before interpreting the ratio.
Use absolute values when the denominator masks business scale.
example: Revenue per user can rise after low-usage customers leave even though no remaining customer spends more.

title: Capacity is set by the bottleneck
summary: In a linked process, total output is constrained by the lowest effective capacity, not the average capacity.
principles: Convert each step to the same output unit and time period.
Identify the lowest effective capacity after downtime and yield loss.
Improve the constraint before adding capacity elsewhere.
example: Adding ovens does not raise bakery output when packaging remains the slowest stage.

title: The math answer is not the business answer
summary: A calculation gives a threshold or outcome; the recommendation must also address feasibility, risk, and action.
principles: Compare the result with a realistic operating or market benchmark.
Test whether the required behavior is commercially achievable.
Recommend what to do, under which condition, and what to validate next.
example: Break-even at 4,000 customers is useful only after judging whether 4,000 reachable customers will actually buy.
